newsitem.title: bosnia: Bildt slamms Yugo endorsement of Serb accord.
newsitem.headline: Bildt slamms Yugo endorsement of Serb accord.

text.p: Carl Bildt, the International High Representative in Bosnia, said on Friday that the Yugoslav parliament had violated the Dayton peace accord by endorsing special ties with the Bosnian Serbs.

Bildt said Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, had been notified that an agreement on closer military and economic ties signed on February 28 was not consistent with Bosnia's peace accord and its constitution.

"By totally disregarding this, the regime in Belgrade has demonstrated that it is not fully committed to the peace agreement for Bosnia, but is prepared to disregard it when this suits its interest," Bildt said in a statement.

The Bosnian Serb parliament also voted for the agreement last weekend, ignoring international and Moslem-Croat criticism that they had no authority to sign defence pacts without prior approval from Bosnia's joint parliament.
Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic told the newspaper Glas Srpski on Friday she would not promulgate into law the agreement on special paralell ties between Bosnian Serbs and Yugoslavia.

She said she had asked for article 14, which provides for the accord to be ratified by the Bosnian multi-ethnic parliament, to be struck from the agreement, claiming it violated the Bosnian Serb constitution.

"The Dayton agreement provides for special parallel ties and puts them in the competence of the entity," Plavsic said, adding that she saw no reason for giving up a degree of Bosnian Serb sovereignty.
Under terms of a 1995 peace agreement, Bosnia is comprised of a Serb republic and a Moslem-Croat federation which have representatives in the central presidency, cabinet and parliament.

The accord between Belgrade and the Bosnian Serb Republic in Pale includes better economic relations and a separate pact that stipulates that neither side would allow its territory to be used for aggression against the other.
International officials fear it may lead to a possible merger between the Serb-controlled territory in Bosnia and Serbia.
Leaders of the Serb republic have been eager to strengthen links with the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro, which have actively supported their rebellion against Bosnia's independence.
The accord is also seen as an attempt to defrost relations damaged by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's pressure on Bosnian Serbs to cave in to international demands for peace talks in 1994.
Even the constitution of the Serb republic has been violated in getting the accord endorsed by the Serb parliament, Bildt said.
"There is hardly a relevant provision in the constitution of Republika Srpska which has not been disregarded or violated in the effort to hammer this procedure through," he said.
"The procedures now seen in both Belgrade and Pale...will affect the attitude of the international community towards them," Bildt said without further elaboration.
